summary: This standards-track memo adds new public key algorithms to the Secure Shell protocol so RSA keys can be used with SHA-256 and SHA-512 for server and client authentication. It updates RFC 4252 and RFC 4253. This lets SSH keep using existing RSA keys while moving away from the older SHA-1 hash.

plainLanguage.summary: Your old key still fits the lock, but now the lock checks it with a stronger stamp. SSH can use the same RSA keys with a better fingerprint method.

questions: how to use rsa keys with sha-256 in ssh
can i keep using my rsa key with sha-256 in ssh
subtitle: How SSH keeps your existing RSA keys while moving signatures from SHA-1 to SHA-256 and SHA-512.

tldr.problem: SSH originally signed with RSA and SHA-1 under the name ssh-rsa, and SHA-1 is now considered deficient. People still have lots of RSA keys they want to keep using.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines two new public key algorithm names, rsa-sha2-256 and rsa-sha2-512. They reuse the ssh-rsa key format unchanged but sign with SHA-256 or SHA-512 using RSASSA-PKCS1-v1_5.
tldr.outcome: Existing RSA keys and trusted fingerprints keep working with stronger hashes. Implementations SHOULD start disabling ssh-rsa by default once the new algorithms are widely adopted.

today: RFC 8332 is a Proposed Standard. The unit metadata shows no RFC obsoleting or updating it. It updates RFC 4252 and RFC 4253.

sections.title: Why SSH Needed New RSA Algorithms
sections.content:
In RFC 4253, SSH defined the public key algorithms ssh-rsa (RSA with SHA-1) and ssh-dss (1024-bit DSA with SHA-1). The RFC calls these algorithms deficient. For US government use, NIST has disallowed 1024-bit RSA and DSA and the use of SHA-1 for signing.

This memo updates RFC 4252 and RFC 4253. It defines new public key algorithms so that existing and new RSA keys can be used, interoperably, with SHA-256 and SHA-512.
sections.plainLanguage: The old way of stamping your name is easy to fake these days. This RFC gives SSH a better stamp that works with the same keys.

sections.title: Key Format Versus Key Algorithm
sections.content:
In RFC 4252, a public key algorithm name ties together three things: (A) how a key pair is generated and validated, (B) the format used to encode a public key, and (C) how a signature is calculated, encoded and verified.

This RFC adds the term public key format for A and B alone. The term public key algorithm still covers all three. The split matters because one key format can now be paired with several signature algorithms.
sections.plainLanguage: A key is like a house key, and the algorithm is also the way you turn it in the lock. This RFC says the same key shape can be turned in new ways.

sections.title: The Two New Algorithms
sections.content:
Two algorithms are defined: rsa-sha2-256, which is RECOMMENDED, and rsa-sha2-512, which is OPTIONAL. Both are for signing, and both work with a raw RSA key. They can be used for server authentication in the transport layer and for client authentication in the authentication layer.

RSA keys do not depend on the hash function, so the new algorithms reuse the ssh-rsa public key format: the string ssh-rsa, then the mpint values e and n. Even the encoded string ssh-rsa stays, so existing keys need no re-encoding and already trusted key fingerprints are unaffected.

Signing and verifying follow RSASSA-PKCS1-v1_5 from RFC 8017, with SHA-256 for rsa-sha2-256 and SHA-512 for rsa-sha2-512. The signature is encoded as the algorithm name followed by an rsa_signature_blob string. That blob holds an octet string S with the same length in octets as the RSA modulus. Some signers omit leading zeros of S, and a verifier MAY accept such shorter encodings.
sections.plainLanguage: The key stays exactly the same. Only the stamp it makes changes, and you pick a bigger stamp (SHA-256 or SHA-512) to make forgery harder.

sections.title: Server and Client Authentication
sections.content:
For server authentication, a client or server lists rsa-sha2-256 and/or rsa-sha2-512 in the server_host_key_algorithms name-list of the SSH_MSG_KEXINIT packet. If one is negotiated, the server sends an ssh-rsa public key during key exchange (for example in SSH_MSG_KEXDH_REPLY) and signs with the matching algorithm name.

For client authentication, the client sends SSH_MSG_USERAUTH_REQUEST with the publickey method and puts rsa-sha2-256 or rsa-sha2-512 in the public key algorithm name field. The public key blob still uses the ssh-rsa format.

If the client includes a signature, it MUST use the same algorithm name inside the signature as in the request. A server that sees a mismatch MAY apply arbitrary authentication penalties, including failure or disconnect. The RFC notes that OpenSSH 7.2 (but not 7.2p2) wrongly writes ssh-rsa in the signature even though SHA-256 or SHA-512 was really used, and a server MAY, but need not, accept that variant.
sections.plainLanguage: When you show your key, you also say which stamp you used, and the stamp has to say the same thing. If the two disagree, the guard may turn you away.

sections.title: Finding What a Server Supports
sections.content:
Experience showed that some servers punish clients who try a public key algorithm the server does not support. To avoid blind guessing, servers that accept rsa-sha2-* signatures for client authentication SHOULD implement the extension negotiation of RFC 8308, especially the server-sig-algs extension.

When a server does not implement server-sig-algs, clients MAY default to an ssh-rsa signature to avoid penalties. Once the new algorithms are widely enough adopted to warrant disabling ssh-rsa, clients MAY default to one of them instead.
sections.plainLanguage: Before trying a stamp, ask the guard which stamps he accepts. If he will not say, use the old one so he does not get cross.

sections.title: IANA Registry Changes
sections.content:
IANA updated the Public Key Algorithm Names table in the Secure Shell (SSH) Protocol Parameters registry from RFC 4250. A new column, Public Key Format, was added to the right of the algorithm name. Existing entries got the same value as their algorithm name.

Two entries were added right after ssh-rsa: rsa-sha2-256 and rsa-sha2-512, both with the public key format ssh-rsa and a reference to this RFC, Section 3.
sections.plainLanguage: The official list of names gets two new lines, and a new column that says which key shape each name uses.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The security considerations of RFC 4251 apply. NIST Special Publication 800-131A, Revision 1 disallows RSA and DSA keys shorter than 2048 bits for US government use and disallows SHA-1 for signature generation, except under NIST's protocol-specific guidance. The RFC says it is prudent to follow this advice outside US government use too.

The document assumes a gradual, compatible transition is better received than an abrupt one. Implementations should add the new algorithms together with SSH_MSG_EXT_INFO and server-sig-algs, but SHOULD start disabling ssh-rsa in default configurations as soon as the new algorithms look widely adopted.

It chooses RSASSA-PKCS1-v1_5 padding because RSASSA-PSS is not universally available, PKCS #1 v1.5 is widely supported in SSH, and it is not known to be insecure for this use. Verifiers MUST NOT apply the RSA key to the signature and then parse the output to extract the hash. They MUST instead apply PKCS1-v1_5 padding to the expected hash and compare the encoded bytes with the RSA output.
sections.plainLanguage: Switch to the stronger stamp, but do it gently so nobody gets locked out. When checking a stamp, rebuild what it should look like and compare, rather than trusting what the stamp says about itself.

data.title: SSH_MSG_USERAUTH_REQUEST encoding
data.code:
byte      SSH_MSG_USERAUTH_REQUEST
string    user name
string    service name
string    "publickey"
boolean   TRUE
string    "rsa-sha2-512"
string    public key blob:
    string    "ssh-rsa"
    mpint     e
    mpint     n
string    signature:
    string    "rsa-sha2-512"
    string    rsa_signature_blob
